13756:
Ronaldo wrote:
>>
line 85 has "for" and "to" in lowercase. These words were probably
"tokenized"
>>

This is not an error; It would be correct to tokenize these BASIC keywords.  It was a regular practice to use Bally BASIC commands inside quotes to save a few bytes.  In this case, using the keywords "FOR" and "TO" (which each only require one bytes each when tokenized) would save three bytes.  That not a big savings, but reserving space was very important when you only had 1,800 bytes to work with in total.

Adam

I added the Bally BASIC 1-player game "Hamurabi" by Richard Houser.  This program was printed in ARCADIAN 2, no. 4 (Feb. 25, 1980): 32-33.  It was also included on the "Best of Arcadian - 1980" tape.

Push any key after the castle appears. You are the King, and you must make decisions on running the kingdom economically. You start with 100 people, 1000 acres of land, and 3000 bushels of food. Buy and sell land, using food as barter material, saving some food to feed the populace. Gain performance points based on how well you govern. If you last ten years, you have done well. Of course, we have thrown in a few random disasters to keep it from being too easy...

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/Hamurabi%20(Houser)(BB).zip

Archiving Notes:

Hamurabi (as printed) (1980)(Richard Houser)(300 baud)(PD).zip - As it was printed in The Arcadian, the program runs out of memory.

Hamurabi (smaller size) (1980)(Richard Houser)(300 baud)(PD).zip - Arcadian program found in Ken Lill's tape collection. Includes space-saving modifications needed to free up memory.

This game has been available in AstroBASIC format for 13 years.  Since AstroBASIC is so much more common than the Bally BASIC cart, why not try that version of the game if you have access to the Bally Arcade hardware, but not the 300-BAUD tape interface:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/hamurabi_%5Bdick_houser%5D.zip

Enjoy!

For some reason Fred Cornett took a liking to me and published everything I sent him whereas Bob Fabris never did. I never knew why but I was very aware of the bad feelings between them. Arcadian was, therefore, Brett’s venue and Cursor became mine. I never met either guy that I recall unless Fabris was at the Wizard Release in Chicago in 1982 or 1983. Fred was very paranoid about Cursor being copied and tried every trick in the book to make it Xerox-proof from printing it in “Copy-Not Blue” to printing it with alternating green and yellow bars across the pages. 13773:
I added Stephen Edwards' 2005 paper called "Reverse Engineering Robby Roto."  Here is some information on the article that I quoted from the paper's abstract:

"Robby Roto was an arcade game produced by Bally/Midway in 1981. Although not especially popular at the time, it does have the distinction of being one of the few commercial arcade games whose code is now in the public domain (the rights reverted to the author Jay [now Jamie] Fenton1, who released it in 1999). Although primitive by today’s standards, it is representative of many early arcade games and illustrates a realistic, commercial embedded system.

"The description presented here has been synthesized from many sources, including disassembled ROM images; source code from MAME2, the multiple arcade machine emulator by Nicola Salmoria and many others; service manuals; and documentation on the Bally Astrocade home video game system3, which contains many of the same custom chips.

"Like many arcade games, Robby was one of a family built with similar hardware. Specifically, it shares its general design with Seawolf II (1978), Space Zap (1980), Extra Bases (1980),Wizard ofWor (1980), Gorf (1981), Professor Pac-Man (1983), and most interestingly, the Bally Astrocade home video game system (1978). All use the same microprocessor, a Zilog Z80, and the same custom graphics and sound chips, which were designed in part by Dave Nutting. For more history of these games and many others, see Herman [2] and Kent [3]."

You can download the paper, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Arcade_Games/Arcade_Games.html#ReverseEngineeringRobbyRoto

13784:
DON'T buy that capacitor kit if the picture is the actual parts! The "monster" cap there is nowhere in the unit, I can't see the value or rating of the brown one, so your guess is as good as mine. and most of the "small" ones are over rated, which is not a good thing for what they are supposed to do. If the parts list calls for a 16 Volt cap and you replace it with a 50V cap, you won't get the best filtering.. You can use a 25Volt or if it calls for a 10 Volt cap, you could theoretically go as high as 25 Volt but I would recommend around 16Volt. You can go somewhat higher on the value (uFD) say 2200 for a 1600, but once again too much of a good thing is not really good.
NEVER go lower in value as this will probably either not work as good (lower uFD) or could explode (lower Voltage).Also, make sure that the minus side is always hooked up to where the minus was on the original. Wrong hookup here is almost always going to explode or start a fire!Please be careful when replacing any parts. Most of these boards were manufactured 40 years ago. you could literally wipe out all IC's by doing the wrong thing. Ask me how I know THAT!?!The last chip on the list was a 7416. These are extremely rare chips with no substitutes! The only ones more rare are the 3 Custom chips: I/O,Address and the Data. The I/O chip was used in several pinball games as well as several video games, but the other 2 were very limited and NO one can make them now. (unless you have about a million dollars to start the process of making new dies for them.Ken

That caps shown in the image are a stock art style arrangement which I use for all leaded-style kits (I have some SMD kits for newer consoles that use different art).  It never occurred to me that it could be interpreted as a photo of exact contents and I've begun the process of altering them to prevent confusion.

The actual caps in the kit are very close to stock values voltage-wise.  The only substitution that I've made recently was changing the 15uf to 22uf caps.  The offerings @ 15uf are more limited and more expensive than 22uf, and in their bypass configuration the change should have no practical effect.

The wiki is set up as a bench repair reference, just useful hand-tailored instant access technical info that should load quickly on even older computers.  I'm starting the process of adding a Common Faults section to all devices and contributions are welcomed & given attribution.

I love supporting the often unsupported devices and I'm always looking for unique products to offer.  Some interesting products have come and go for the Astrocade and if anyone has something to offer but doesn't want to handle the retail end please keep me in mind!

Thanks,
Luke

Here are some Bally Arcade/Astrocade "homebrew" items that exist (or have been sold in the past).  It would be great to see some of these items get a re-release:

I) Astrocade Multicarts:

1) Astrocade Multicart (by CPUWIZ) - Released in 2004.  No longer available.

2) Astrocade Multicart (by GaMBITS) - This multicart is also known as the "UltiMulti Cartridge" contains more software than any of the other Astrocade multicarts.  Released in 2007 or 2008.  I think that Ken Lill has stopped making these.  Is that right, Ken?

3) Astrocade Multicart (by RetroKidz) - Released in 2006. Once available from 8-Bit Domain.  No longer available.

4) Astrocade Multicart (by Ward Shrake) - Released in 2002.  No longer available.

More information on the Multicarts can be read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/multicarts/multicarts.html


II) Astrocade Homebrew Cartridges:

5) "Crazy Climber" - Homebrew cart limited to 50 copies.  Programmed by Michael Garber.  Released in 2011.  No longer available.

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/Crazy%20Climber%20Manual%20%282012%29%28Riff%20Raff%20Games%29.pdf

6) "War" (by RiffRaff Games) - Homebrew cart limited to 50 copies (the first run was 20 carts and the second run had 30 carts).  Programmed by Michael Garber.  Released in 2007.  No longer available.

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/box_pics/riff_riff_games/riff_riff_games.html


III) Astrocade Cartridges in the Public Domain:

Two cartridges were officially been released into the public domain in 2001 by Brett Bilbrey:

7) ICBM Attack (Released by Spectre Systems) - A 4K third-party cartridge.   This game requires a special controller.  No instructions have been archived for this game.

Here is what the ICBM Attack controller looks like:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/ICBM_Attack_Handle/ICBM_Attack_Handle.html

ICBM Attack can be played in an emulator with a special setup.  Here's how:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/Playing_ICBM_Attack_Using_MESS.pdf


8) Treasure Cove (By Brett Bilbrey) - An 8K third-party cartridge.

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/treasure%20cove%20%28instructions%29%28color%29%28300%20dpi%29.pdf

The article about the release of these two cartridges into the public domain is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/two_astrocade_pd_programs.html

There is plenty of information from Brett Bilbrey's archives on Spectre Systems:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/spectre_systems/spectre_systems.html


IV) Public Domain Software:

There has been plenty of programs released for the Astrocade into the public domain.  Maybe these can be compiled into special sets and released on an audio CD with versions of the programs that can be loaded into Bally BASIC and/or AstroBASIC.

A VERY outdated listing (from 2002!) of the PD software is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_pd_faq.txt

Paul Thacker would be able to fill in other software that has been made available through the years.  Yes, that PD list needs a MAJOR overhaul.

Here is a list of some of the software in the above PD FAQ.  This listing doesn't cover all of the PD software, but these are some of the major highlights:

10) "Arcadian" Newsletter - All of the type-in programs published in the Arcadian were made freely distributable on April 13, 2001 by Robert Fabris.  Here is a collection of many of the AstroBASIC games available from the Arcadian:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/arcadian.html

11) George Moses Co. - Software released into the public domain July 23, 2001 by George Moses.  It would be great to have audio CDs of each of the music tapes created by George.  I've actually created three (of five) professional-looking CDs for myself (and a few others, distributed among Astrocade friends of mine) .  Here are the songs created by Mr. Moses:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/george_moses/george_moses.html

12) New Image - Software released as PostcardWare on August 2, 2001 by Don Gladden.  I guess, technically, this isn't public domain, but it is free.  If you use the software, then you should send a postcard to Don... wherever he lives now.  New Image released MANY tapes for the Astrocade.  Here are some of their AstroBASIC releases:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/new_image/new_image.html

13) Wavemakers - Software released into the public domain on August 7, 2001 by Mike Peace.  WaveMakers made about 20 tapes, some with more than one program on them.  These games are usually considered some of the best BASIC games on the system; actually, a few of them are considered among the best games on the Astrocade of ANY kind!

Here is a listing of some of WaveMaker's AstroBASIC games:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/WaveMakers/WaveMakers.html

In 2007, Paul Thacker archived ALL of the original master copies of the tapes by WaveMakers.  Here's an article about how that came about:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/How%20the%20Wavemakers%20'Masters'%20Update%20Come%20About%20%282007%29%28Paul%20Thacker%29.txt

IV) Hardware:

14) Lil' White Ram - 32K Ram Expansion created by Mike White and Ken Lill.  Released in 2008.  No longer available.  A great upgrade that allows the Astrocade user to run many of RAM expansion programs written in the early-to-mid 1980s for Vipersoft BASIC (and some, for Blue Ram BASIC).

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Lil_White_RAM/Lil-White-Ram.html

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/Lil_White_RAM/Lil_White_RAM.html

15) Astrocade S-Video Upgrade - Developed by 8-Bit Domain and released in 2006.  No longer available.

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/s-video_mod/s-video_mod.html


VI) Homebrew Hardware Protoypes:

Atarimax 512K Maxflash - Michael Di Salvo's dream cartridge!  512K flash memory cartridge created in 2011 by AtariMax (Steven Tucker).  This cart has 128 bankswitched 4K blocks.  This hardware WAS produced for testing; I have one of them.  It's awesome hardware!

This product was under wraps for a LONG time, but Michael allowed it to be talked about semi-recently.  It would be very expensive to produce-- I seem to recall that Steven and Michael's estimate was something like $3,000 to get it this cartridge off the ground.  Michael Garber provided some software/demos for this cart that really show it off!  I created some documentation describing how it works, and what can be used with it.  All of this information (and Michael Gabrer's demo programs) were available on a no longer online website (the website is archived on my hard drive).

I love this cartridge and I hope that it sees a release some day!  Programming the hardware requires no EPROMs (thank goodness).  It can be programmed quickly (and easily) by plugging it into the USB Flashcart programmer created from use with the Atari8-bit cartridges.  This cartridge is unique, as one side of the PCB fits into the Bally Arcade/Astrocade unit, while the other side of the cart features a Atari 8-bit computer cartridge connector.

http://msdconsulting.wix.com/128kgames

http://atariage.com/forums/topic/213554-the-astrocade-512k-bank-switching-cartridge-at-128kgames/

http://www.atarimax.com/flashcart/documentation/


Am I missing anything on this homebrew list of released or announced items?

Wouldn't it be great to see some of these items distributed again (or for the first time)?

Adam

13791:
Hey all,
 

 About 6 months ago I picked up a Retrokidz 72-in-1 multicart on eBay and briefly played with it.  It came with a printout of the DIP switch settings that are posted on the Bally Alley website, and they all seemed to work just fine.  Then it got packed up and I didn't touch it again until today.
 

 Well, now any game that has the second switch from the right set to "1" just gives me gibberish on the main menu.  (For clarity, that's the #7 switch as labeled on the cart, second number from the left on the sheet since they're printed in reverse order on the original sheet).  It starts off by filling up the screen with the letter U, then V, W, X, Y, and Z over time.  I don't remember it doing that before, as I'm pretty sure I was able to load Solar Conqueror and The Incredible Wizard when I initially tested it, and those are near the end of the list with a 1 in that bit.  I could be mistaken, though, since I also have those carts and I may have just played those.
 

 Has anyone else seen this kind of behavior?  Can't imagine why that would have happened short of the multicart's memory becoming corrupted.  If the switch failed I'd expect it to always be on or always be off, not give me weird garbage output.
 

 Doug

New device I’m trying to implement for all old systems, so why not start with Astrocade?:

It’s a way to turn old video games into old online video games by using a low ping connection, specifically Sprint Direct Connect or AT&T or Verizon Push-to-Talk.  If you’re able to beat 8ms, then all you need is a modern machine that can rewind half a frame and deal with network outages, and a couple administrative stuff, and a 100% compatible system, like using an original Astrocade chipset and cartridge reader and controller ports.

It’d basically be a net flashback.   I got a few companies possibly interested taking up this offer but it would be after the provisional patent runs out.   If someone wants to play Incredible Wizard and every other Astrocade multiplayer game online, they should fund this project.  One of those companies is Sega.   Another is Atari.  I’ve been trying to get a hold of WB Games (who, because they bought Bally/Midway, should be the owners of the Astrocade for today’s purposes) but never got anywhere beyond the customer support

Minimum of what I need is $5000 for the patent extension. Maximum of what I need is $30,000 for the patent plus patying a prototype builder to build a prototype based on this description.   It can be as low as $10,000 for both the patent extension and the prototypes.

If I can’t get this from one company, maybe someone can raise money for this using kickstarter.com   I shouldn’t use it because I have nothing to offer donors.  It’s only based on the idea that this would be a cool thing to have exist.    And I can’t seem to get support without paying someone rewards, or I’d have to factor in premium prices into what I’m raising to pay for gifts.

Anyone interested post to Bally Alley forums.   I can’t offer percentage of the profits on the concept for funding it on kickstarter, but I could on Bally Alley.  Any serious offers, email me, Brian Ciesicki, at tripletopper@earthlink.net.

Hey all,


About 6 months ago I picked up a Retrokidz 72-in-1 multicart on eBay and briefly played with it.  It came with a printout of the DIP switch settings that are posted on the Bally Alley website, and they all seemed to work just fine.  Then it got packed up and I didn't touch it again until today.


Well, now any game that has the second switch from the right set to "1" just gives me gibberish on the main menu.  (For clarity, that's the #7 switch as labeled on the cart, second number from the left on the sheet since they're printed in reverse order on the original sheet).  It starts off by filling up the screen with the letter U, then V, W, X, Y, and Z over time.  I don't remember it doing that before, as I'm pretty sure I was able to load Solar Conqueror and The Incredible Wizard when I initially tested it, and those are near the end of the list with a 1 in that bit.  I could be mistaken, though, since I also have those carts and I may have just played those.


Has anyone else seen this kind of behavior?  Can't imagine why that would have happened short of the multicart's memory becoming corrupted.  If the switch failed I'd expect it to always be on or always be off, not give me weird garbage output.


Doug

I'll add these to the public domain FAQ sometime soon.  Dave gave permission to place his software into the public domain in his interview that was posted on February 27, 2006:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/interviews/interview_with_david_ibach.txt

It would be great to see a rerelease of "Sneaky Snake," a truly rare Centipede clone that is fun to play.  This game was programmed using Dave's own assembler that runs on the Bally Arcade/Astrocade, "General Video Assembler."

Here's a picture of the official "Sneaky Snake" cart that I used to own (sorry it's such a low resolution picture-- it was posted to Bally Alley back in the early 2000s):

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Third-Party%29/full_size/sneaky_snake.jpg

Even though the above cart looks like a rip-off (the old Bally Label is under it!), I have been told that some of the early cartridges were made like this at an Astro-Bash in the early 80s.  Here is a picture of a "Sneaky Snake" that I found many years ago on Ebay that doesn't have the an old label under it:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Third-Party%29/full_size/Sneaky%20Snake%20%28a1%29.jpg

Finally, here is a clean-up label of "Sneaky Snake:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Third-Party%29/full_size/Sneaky%20Snake%20%28Label%29.jpg

Here is a screenshot of "Sneaky Snake:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/screenshots/cart_screenshots/s/sneaky_snake.gif

I don't think that any instructions for "Sneaky Snake" have surfaced, but if some existed then they must have said something like, "Fire at the baddie and get points!"

"General Video Assembler" has been covered before-- Paul tested it extensively.  This program wouldn't need a rerelease, but it's neat that it's available for those who are interested in it.  He's the manual for the assembler:

http://www.ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/dave_ibach/docs-general_video_assembler.pdf

Thanks to Paul for pointing out this additional PD software!

Adam

There is probably only a few reasons that an EPROM would lose it's data.1) getting an over-voltage spike.2) Solar flair type of radiation ( or maybe a lot of light from a fluorescent light. which is highly unlikely due to the opacity of the cartridge shell)  and3) Keeping it stored in an area that has very little moisture, like the dessert. Static electricity can build up in the air and short out between the leads. Because there is no buffer in these carts and the inputs are high impedance, it theoretically is possible.4) The last is just age. The circuitry inside an EPROM is made so that they can be erased and reprogrammed. This circuitry has a tendency to "fade" over 10-20 years. That is why so many electronic devices give out over a period of time.just some fuel for thought.

If the switch is the culprit, It makes sense also. You are trying to access a part of the EPROM that isn't where it should be, causing data errors. It probably isn't shorted, but may not be making contact.There may also be something loose inside, or originally soldered poorly.These are the reasons I can think of that may cause the problem.

I would take the shell apart and look for anything out of the ordinary. Then, if you have a meter, check poth positions of the switch (the contacts are across from each other). If you get an open, that will probably be your problem. Replacing that whole switch would be the solution.
Ken

>>

If it's a bad chip, then you are correct, there isn't much that you can do yourself without an EPROM burner (presuming that it DOES use an EPROM-- maybe it uses an EEPROM?).  Plus, as Ken seems to infer (I think), you don't have the 256K (or 512K, or whatever is the correct size) of the ROM image that was burned onto the original chip.  Which doesn't mean that you can't create your own ROM image with your own files using the dumps available from BallyAlley.com.

I think that all of the Astrocade multicarts have the ROM chips soldered to them because the carts are too narrow to allow a socket, which is a shame.  Ward Shrake's Arcadia 2001 multicart used a socket, and he found upgrading someone's Arcadia 2001 multicart a breeze compared to upgrading an Astrocade multicart to a new ROM image.

It might be easiest to contact the seller and see if there is anything that he can do for you to repair your cart.  Like I mentioned about my Atari 5200 multicart: Sean Kelly was able to repair my dead multicart (that he made) for a very nominal fee, and this was done many years after I bought the multicart from him.  Perhaps this other person would be just as kind to you.  Wouldn't that be nice?  Remember, it's the giving time of year: spirits are high and many people are full of cheer.  Maybe this will be one of Retrokidz' small good deeds this year...?

Adam

Thanks to the kind permission of Michael Di Salvo, I have archived the Atarimax Maxflash Astrocade Cartridge website (formerly known as bally128k.com or "Bally/Astrocade Maxflash Files") to BallyAlley.com. This website was previously for owners, users and developers of the prototype flash cartridge for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  Even though this cartridge has not been released (yet?), all of the documentation and programs have been archived for reference for anyone that is interested in knowing more about this project.

You can view the archived version of the site, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/bally128k-com/maxflash/maxflash.htm

Note that all the programs on the site, the documentation and all of the other information is live.  You can download it and read it all to discover what this fantastic project is all about.  Note that all of the programs require the MaxFlash cart to use them properly.

Here is what Michael Di Salvo says about the public release of the documentation and programs for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

"Of course, feel free to add [the website to BallyAlley.com] as you see fit.  Although technically its not 'defunct' in that its still online and I have never officially shelved plans for the flashcart.  Same reason I've never asked everybody to mail them back to me as I still have hopes to one day do something with it.

"If you want to do a write up about it how it developed and stuff please feel free to do so.  That way ten years down the road when someone posts on the yahoo group 'hey how come nobody every made a bank switched cart for the Astrocade' you can point them in the right direction.

You can visit Michael's current website that covers this bankswitched cart.  His site is meant for end-users to see, rather than being directed to people who are working on the bankswitched cart project.

http://msdconsulting.wix.com/128kgames

As Michael used to like to say in the early stages of the cartridge development, "128K. Your Life Will Never Be The Same."  Now that the cartridge is actually 512K of bankswitched memory, Michael's' quote needs to be updated to something like, "512k.  It's a Fat Arcade."  I guess might not make sense to many of you.  It would only be funny for those that remember that the original 128K Apple Macintosh was called the "Fat Mac" when it had 512K installed into it.  (Wow, it's amazing to think that ANY Mac shipped with just 128K of memory.)

Enjoy the website, and I've love to hear comments from anyone that browses through the information and files.

13815:
Merry Christmas, folks!  For those that don't celebrate the Christmas... then happy holidays!

It's that time of year again when you sit around a fireplace (when you can), get a glass of egg nog (with some (or a lot!) of rum), cuddle-up close to a loved one and have some holiday fun by playing a few of the 27 songs Christmas-themed songs transcribed for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  That's right, it's time for:

"27 Christmas Carols" by George Moses.  This was his second tape of music that he transcribed for the Astrocade.  It's got "All your favorites. Some with vibrato."

You can listen to all the songs (in mp3 format) here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/george_moses/27_Christmas_Carols_%5BTape_2%5D/christmas.html

BallyAlley.com isn't setup up for streaming music, but it may still work to some degree.  You're best bet to listen to this music (without possible stutter) is to save the song locally to you computer (if you can).  If you can't, then the song should start playing eventually when it's done downloading.

Here is more information about the tape:

Tape 2: 27 Christmas Carols by George Moses Co.
     "Our all time best-seller! All your favorites in 3-part harmony, some with vibrato. 27 programs on one tape!"
          - Arcadian, Vol 4, No. 12, Pg. 122.

The Christmas songs for download are listed in alphabetical order.  The original
playing order for the tape, 27 Christmas Carols, is:

Side 1

1)  Oh Christmas Tree (Oh Tannenbaum)
2)  Silent Night, Holy Night - By Franz Gruber
3)  Deck the Hall
4)  Away in a Manger
5)  Here We Come A-Wassailing - Ernest Stevens
6)  Jolly Old St Nicholas
7)  Up on the Rooftop - Hanby
8)  Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring - Johann Sebastian Bach
9)  We Three Kings of Orient Are - J.H. Hopkins Jr.
10) O Come, All Ye Faithful
11) Lullaby, Thou Little Tiny Child
12) Joy To the World - George F. Handel
13) What Child is This (Greensleeves)
14) The First Noel

Side 2

1)  Hark the Herald Angels Sing
2)  Angels We Have Heard On High
3)  O Come, O Come Immanuel
4)  Good King Wenceslas
5)  March of the Toys
6)  It Came Upon a Midnight Clear
7)  Toyland
8)  God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen
9)  Jingle Bells
10) O Little Town of Bethlehem
11) We Wish You a Merry Christmas
12) Prepare Thyself Zion
13) Auld Lang Syne

Want to really nerd-out?  Then why not play a few of these tunes directly from you Astrocade!  You can download the programs, transfer them to the BASIC cartridge and then listen to your Astrocade sing away the holiday!

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/george_moses/christmas_tape/christmas_tape.html

Here is the original ad for the Moses' Christmas tape:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_3/arcadian_vol_03_issue_01.pdf#Page=9

Here are advertisements for some of the music available from George Moses:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_12.pdf#Page=8

http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/George%20Moses%20Software%20%28Ad%29%28Tapes%201-5%29.pdf

Wanna catch up with George, via 1982...?  Then here is an interesting article about him called "This Moses Wants to Lead You to the Video Land" from the March 10,1982 issue of "The Brighton Argus" newspaper:

http://www.ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/This%20Moses%20Wants/This%20Moses%20Wants%20%28March%2010%201982%29%28Bob%20Gritzinger%29%28The%20Brighton%20Argus%29.pdf

Happy holidays to all of you Astrocade fans... and a special thanks to George Moses for putting so much of his personal time and effort into creating this Christmas music and allowing it to be shared with the entire Astrocade community by his placing it into the public domain.  George took his game system, his BASIC programming cartridge and  looked at it from a different angle.  He transcribed directly from sheet music to numbers typed into his Astrocade late into the night.  Eventurally he was able to say, "When you're through playing 'Space Invaders'... play 'Silent Night' on your Bally Arcade!"

Have a great Christmas... and I hope that you all get some classic gaming fun in today.

One of the first "articles" that I put on BallyAlley.com was a collection of two columns asking (and answering) whatever happened to the Bally Arcade, Interact and VideoBrain computer systems.  I never knew the exact source of the columns.  Today I did some research (now that many complete "Creative Computing" magazines are online) and I figured it out.  Here are the sources of the two columns, both by David H. Ahl

1) "Where are they now? Bally, Interact and VideoBrain," CREATIVE COMPUTING, 6, no. 9 (Sept. 1980): 38.

2) "Follow up: Bally, Interact and VideoBrain," CREATIVE COMPUTING, 7, no. 3 (Mar 1981): 48,50.

I had supposed that the follow-up column had appeared in the very next issue of the magazine.  It actually took nearly six months for people to get more information.  What a wait that must have been!

The first column poses the question to readers asking what happened to the three computer systems.  The follow-up column has the answers along with places to get information about two of the systems.  Even in 1981, one of the systems, the VideoBrain from 1977, was long dead.  Readers' response to Ahl's request for Videobrain information was underwhelming.  Here is what Mr. Ahl heard back about the VideoBrain: "Nothing, zip, zero.  People wrote to us wondering where to get cartridges, repairs, et al.  But that was it.  No one gave us any leads to current dealers or sources.  It's almost as though the company, their dealers and most of their customers vanished to another planet."

Luckily, Bally Arcade owners were much luckier!  There were plenty of resources for that soon-to-be-christened system called the Bally Astrocade (the hardware was about to get a re-released in 1981 courtesy of Astrovision, Inc.).

This historical information makes it plain just how difficult it was for people to get information about their orphaned computer systems.  Owners today have a much easier time getting information about long-gone computer systems then owners did even when their systems were near-new.

The original pdf of these columns was created from poor photocopies, and the exact date of the columns was unknown.  This has been rectified.  I've ripped the two color magazine covers and three grayscale pages from the complete magazines and have made an entirely new document out of them, which you can read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/articles_and_news.html#BallyInteractVideoBrain

I've always considered these two, short columns must-reads.  They allow us to glimpse what many 70s-era computer systems were already facing: computer obsolesce.  If you've missed reading two columns these up to now, then this is a perfect opportunity to try to wrap your head around those long-ago, bygone, some may say, golden years  of the early computer era.

Adam suggested I introduce myself to the group and give a little background. My name's Nathan, I was first introduced to the Astrocade via my late employer. When he was young, he and a partner had a small business refurbing defective Bally boards in Chicago for Midway (I guess.) I don't know too much that business, except that it was located on Elston Avenue. Many years later I bought him an Astrocade on eBay as a nostalgic semi-gag gift, and in the process of testing it decided that I wanted one for myself! (Incredible Wizard sealed the deal.)  I'm an electronics technician with my own shop refurbing high end audio gear. Aside from the Astrocade, I don't do any other retro-gaming stuff, but it's a fun joint activity to do with my son!
     I recently bought one of those 72 in 1 multicarts and became intrigued with the idea of playing ICBM attack with an original Spectre handle. I've now got a crude working substitute.  I had an X-Y joystick controller with dual 100K ohm pots. I paralleled 100K fixed resistors with the pots to get the resistance to the correct value (50K) for the Astrocade. One pot goes to Astrocade port one, one pot goes to Astrocade port two. This part works great!  I eventually figured out that you need to use the trigger switch which is attached to port 2 to start the gameplay. You can then fire the left missile using a left switch closure on Port 1, the center missile using the trigger switch closure on Port 1 and the right missile using the right switch closure port 1.  Looking at pictures of the original Spectre handle, I see that it has buttons on both sides, so I'm guessing that the left "pinball" button was for firing the left missile, the right "pinball" button the right missile, but I don't really know which buttons on the keypad were used to fire the center missile or start the gameplay. I guess it doesn't really matter, I'm not trying to build an exact replica, but I'd like to at least confirm that I have the basic setup and operation of the controller correct- if anyone has tried it with the Spectre Systems controller and can share that info, that would be great.  I'm happy to share more details of my build if anyone else would like to make one. Basically, you need an X-Y joystick with 100K pots, a couple of resistors, four switches and a pair of DB-9 connectors/cables to make a minimal replica.

Does anyone have any "starting out" easy advice?  I also do not know exactly how to remove the RF shield.  All links I can find to this and the service manual seem to be outdated.OK, here's what you can try. Because heat can cause the problem, it really is hard to figure our which part is breaking down.The RF shield is usually easy to remove. 1st remove the top cover by removing the 5 black screws on the bottom. Now the shield is in sight. There were about 5 different shields made over the years. The hardest to remove is the full sized one. It is the one that goes under the cartridge area. It you have that one, please reply to this. Assuming that you have one of the shorter ones, 1st remove the clips on the sides. If you can pick it up near the cartridge area, remove the copper strips that tie it to various things. This should be easy, the glue is over 30 years old! If you have a soldering iron, melt the solder in the area of the hand control ports until it is free. Then just discard it. If you don't have a soldering iron, then by bending it back and forth multiple times usually does the job. Don't try to tear it off, you may cause damage to the unit.The next job ( or first if you have a full size shield) is to remove the plastic piece that has the keypad and cassette slot. There are 4 screws to remove the unit from the bottom plastic, located in the corners. now carefully lift the unit out of the plastic by lifting the "front" side out and sliding the unit slightly forward and then out.There are 4 screws holding in the keypad plastic. They may be either 1/4 inch hex / slotted or Phillips.Carefully lift the plastic from the front, like you did with the unit, except that this won't come free all the way. The keypad switch PCB IS STILL CONNECTED. Try to leave this on, but DO NOT bend it back and forth. That would break the wires going to the unit.Now you will be able to see the Custom Data chip and all of the voltage regulators.The ONLY parts you can do a swap with are now all exposed. They are:1) The plug in part of the power supply ( sometimes called a "wall wart") it has a 4 pin connector that plugs into the square metal unit that sticks out one side. We'll call this the left side. swapping these is relative easy.
2)The next is the RF Modulator. It is closer to the front (the back has the hand control ports). It needs to be slid off to the left along with the cable. Swap both.3) Now comes the delicate part. The 3 custom chips.    A) there is the Data chip. It may or may not hav a metal heat sink on it. If it doesn't, there is probably some white slimy stuff (heat sink grease) on the top. It is the chip that was under the keypad. to remove any of the custom chips, you will need a very small screwdriver. Place it between the socket and the chip on the left side. CAREFULLY twist the tool to start separating them. do not bend it all the way up on one end. carefully push the screwdriver towards the other end until the entire chip is loose from the socket. This way you won't bent the pins out of place. Do the same with your second unit, replacing ONE chip at a time. BE CAREFUL to make sure that all pins are straight and that you don't bend any over when putting hem into the socket. B) thene if that doesn't do it, there's the Address chip. it is just back of the keypad wiring. Follow the same procedures as above.C) Last is the I/O chip it is closest to hand controls 1 & 2 sockets. The same procedures apply.Remember, swap only 1 item at a time, so that if you get one working, you'll know what was wrong. If you do more than one, you may be fixing one problem but adding a new on, so you'll never solve the problem.If you get one working, just reverse the order of (dis)assembly.Make sure, before you replace the keypad plastic the the SWITCH PCB is fully in it's slot. If not the keypad may not work.
If you feel to overwhelmed by this, seek out some help doing this. If you break a pin off of any Custom chip, there aren't any on the open market.There are only 2 people with any extra chips, and I am one. If you REALLY need help, contact me : kenzre@yahoo.com
Help is appreciated.  I can tell this is an awesome community. 
If anyone wants to answer a final question, I did get a BASIC interface and I'm wondering if there are any worthwhile games on this format?  I know they are different.
Thanks all!

I'm not sure if I ever posted here but as a newer member I thought I'd pass along my memories of the Bally Astrocade.

In 1977 I saw an ad in Popular Mechanics or some similar magazine. The ad was from JS&A, the original distributor of the Bally Home Library Computer. I ordered one but had to wait until 1978 to receive my first unit. The ad was very enticing.......remember this was 1977 before the PC. There were a couple of other game "consoles" but the Bally was neat. Try to erase anything about "computers" from your mind, then see an ad for the Bally "Computer".  Anyhow I received the "Bally Home Library Computer" opened the box and after an hour it started to fail. I sent it back to JS&A and got another unit. It began to fail in a couple of hours. I then got a 3rd unit. When the Bally was announced in 1977 there were delays one after another until they began to ship them in 1978. My recollection was the units did not meet FCC requirements until they installed a styrofoam shell covered with aluminum foil. Anyhow on the 3rd unit I threw the foil covers out and turned the Bally, waited a minute or so, touched each chip and found ( I think it was 3 chips running hot). I had some heat sinks ( I was a mainframe computer tech and had access to heat sinks) and glued them to the chips. No more heat problems. I added the Basic cartridge and the tape cassette interface. I wrote a couple of Basic language routines (surely nothing to brag about and added a power on light). I joined a Bally Newsletter, got one each month for several months (I think) and that's it. We had the Bally for a couple of years and bought all the cartridges that were released. I sold it to buy a PC but should have kept the Bally Computer. I'm not sure how many units they made before Bally sold the rights and the name was changed to 'Astrocade"? Well that's my experience with the Bally Astrocade. I saw a Bally on ebay a few days ago for sale. The asking price was $599. It looked new. I've seen a few others on ebay, most looked like junk.

Hi Chuck,Don't judge a book by it's cover. Bally and or Asrtocade units are over 30 years old and you should expect some wear and tear on them. What you really want is proof that it is working. Then, when you get it, NEVER play it on a rug, towel or anything that will block the bottom vents, even a little. To make it's chance of lasting longer, buy a laptop cooling fan and put the unit on it. Astrocade never sent theirs out with heat sinks. They lasted much better most Bally's without.There have been quite a few games out that Bally did not release. They came from Astrocade and 3rd party companies.Ken Lill

You still can't get a total linear motion by doing the 2 ends, but it sure is a whole lot closer.

    Adam suggested I introduce myself to the group and give a little background. My name's Nathan, I was first introduced to the Astrocade via my late employer. When he was young, he and a partner had a small business refurbing defective Bally boards in Chicago for Midway (I guess.) I don't know too much that business, except that it was located on Elston Avenue. Many years later I bought him an Astrocade on eBay as a nostalgic semi-gag gift, and in the process of testing it decided that I wanted one for myself! (Incredible Wizard sealed the deal.) I'm an electronics technician with my own shop refurbing high end audio gear. Aside from the Astrocade, I don't do any other retro-gaming stuff, but it's a fun joint activity to do with my son!
 I recently bought one of those 72 in 1 multicarts and became intrigued with the idea of playing ICBM attack with an original Spectre handle. I've now got a crude working substitute. I had an X-Y joystick controller with dual 100K ohm pots. I paralleled 100K fixed resistors with the pots to get the resistance to the correct value (50K) for the Astrocade. One pot goes to Astrocade port one, one pot goes to Astrocade port two. This part works great! I eventually figured out that you need to use the trigger switch which is attached to port 2 to start the gameplay. You can then fire the left missile using a left switch closure on Port 1, the center missile using the trigger switch closure on Port 1 and the right missile using the right switch closure port 1. Looking at pictures of the original Spectre handle, I see that it has buttons on both sides, so I'm guessing that the left "pinball" button was for firing the left missile, the right "pinball" button the right missile, but I don't really know which buttons on the keypad were used to fire the center missile or start the gameplay. I guess it doesn't really matter, I'm not trying to build an exact replica, but I'd like to at least confirm that I have the basic setup and operation of the controller correct- if anyone has tried it with the Spectre Systems controller and can share that info, that would be great. I'm happy to share more details of my build if anyone else would like to make one. Basically, you need an X-Y joystick with 100K pots, a couple of resistors, four switches and a pair of DB-9 connectors/cables to make a minimal replica.

Nathan

    Hello!
I'm Clay.  I'm new to the Astrocade (and this entire hobby in general).  I am, however, enthusiastic about it!  I'm not very technically proficient and, as has been pointed out, tons of folks on here seem to be.  I can do my best though!
I have one easy question: how hard is it to get a hold of the game "Muncher?"  And, along with that, "War"?  I can find these titles nor the multicards.  I blew all my money on my consoles so can't afford much, but wondering where to look for all that.My multiCart has both programs on it. It also has ALL carts, including all of the 3rd party ones. The cost is $125.00 + P&H. ($15.00 in US) more for international.
MORE IMPORTANTLY:
I recently bought TWO "Arcade" consoles.  These were untested but complete, and came with quite a few extras.  They aren't pretty, but (as I presumed) now that I have them most of that can be remedied.  I knew very well what I was getting myself into but hoped for a miracle.  No miracle, but maybe close.  The really ugly unit (which had--no joke--MUD DAUBERS living it it) functions partially.  It will turn on and look perfect for a few seconds, then start getting freaky after about 15 seconds.  I'm presuming this is a "heat" issue, but I don't know for sure.  It doesn't turn off or go black. 
The second unit doesn't power on, or at least gets no signal to the TV.  It looks pristine and I am hoping it is something very simple.  I DID swap adapters and that made no difference. 
Does anyone have any "starting out" easy advice?  I also do not know exactly how to remove the RF shield.  All links I can find to this and the service manual seem to be outdated.OK, here's what you can try. Because heat can cause the problem, it really is hard to figure our which part is breaking down.The RF shield is usually easy to remove. 1st remove the top cover by removing the 5 black screws on the bottom. Now the shield is in sight. There were about 5 different shields made over the years. The hardest to remove is the full sized one. It is the one that goes under the cartridge area. It you have that one, please reply to this. Assuming that you have one of the shorter ones, 1st remove the clips on the sides. If you can pick it up near the cartridge area, remove the copper strips that tie it to various things. This should be easy, the glue is over 30 years old! If you have a soldering iron, melt the solder in the area of the hand control ports until it is free. Then just discard it. If you don't have a soldering iron, then by bending it back and forth multiple times usually does the job. Don't try to tear it off, you may cause damage to the unit.The next job ( or first if you have a full size shield) is to remove the plastic piece that has the keypad and cassette slot. There are 4 screws to remove the unit from the bottom plastic, located in the corners. now carefully lift the unit out of the plastic by lifting the "front" side out and sliding the unit slightly forward and then out.There are 4 screws holding in the keypad plastic. They may be either 1/4 inch hex / slotted or Phillips.Carefully lift the plastic from the front, like you did with the unit, except that this won't come free all the way. The keypad switch PCB IS STILL CONNECTED. Try to leave this on, but DO NOT bend it back and forth. That would break the wires going to the unit.Now you will be able to see the Custom Data chip and all of the voltage regulators.The ONLY parts you can do a swap with are now all exposed. They are:1) The plug in part of the power supply ( sometimes called a "wall wart") it has a 4 pin connector that plugs into the square metal unit that sticks out one side. We'll call this the left side. swapping these is relative easy.
2)The next is the RF Modulator. It is closer to the front (the back has the hand control ports). It needs to be slid off to the left along with the cable. Swap both.3) Now comes the delicate part. The 3 custom chips.    A) there is the Data chip. It may or may not hav a metal heat sink on it. If it doesn't, there is probably some white slimy stuff (heat sink grease) on the top. It is the chip that was under the keypad. to remove any of the custom chips, you will need a very small screwdriver. Place it between the socket and the chip on the left side. CAREFULLY twist the tool to start separating them. do not bend it all the way up on one end. carefully push the screwdriver towards the other end until the entire chip is loose from the socket. This way you won't bent the pins out of place. Do the same with your second unit, replacing ONE chip at a time. BE CAREFUL to make sure that all pins are straight and that you don't bend any over when putting hem into the socket. B) thene if that doesn't do it, there's the Address chip. it is just back of the keypad wiring. Follow the same procedures as above.C) Last is the I/O chip it is closest to hand controls 1 & 2 sockets. The same procedures apply.Remember, swap only 1 item at a time, so that if you get one working, you'll know what was wrong. If you do more than one, you may be fixing one problem but adding a new on, so you'll never solve the problem.If you get one working, just reverse the order of (dis)assembly.Make sure, before you replace the keypad plastic the the SWITCH PCB is fully in it's slot. If not the keypad may not work.
If you feel to overwhelmed by this, seek out some help doing this. If you break a pin off of any Custom chip, there aren't any on the open market.There are only 2 people with any extra chips, and I am one. If you REALLY need help, contact me : kenzre@yahoo.com
Help is appreciated.  I can tell this is an awesome community. 
If anyone wants to answer a final question, I did get a BASIC interface and I'm wondering if there are any worthwhile games on this format?  I know they are different.
Thanks all!
Clay

    I'm not sure if I ever posted here but as a newer member I thought I'd pass along my memories of the Bally Astrocade.

In 1977 I saw an ad in Popular Mechanics or some similar magazine. The ad was from JS&A, the original distributor of the Bally Home Library Computer. I ordered one but had to wait until 1978 to receive my first unit. The ad was very enticing.......remember this was 1977 before the PC. Try to erase anything about "computers" from your mind, then see an ad for the Bally "Computer".  Anyhow I received the "Bally Home Library Computer" opened the box and after an hour it started to fail. I sent it back to JS&A and got another unit. It began to fail in a couple of hours. I then got a 3rd unit. When the Bally was announced in 1977 there were delays one after another until they began to ship them in 1978. My recollection was the units did not meet FCC requirements until they installed a styrofoam shell covered with aluminum foil. Anyhow on the 3rd unit I threw the foil covers out and turned the Bally, waited a minute or so, touched each chip and found ( I think it was 3 chips running hot). I had some heat sinks ( I was a mainframe computer tech and had access to heat sinks) and glued them to the chips. No more heat problems. I added the Basic cartridge and the tape cassette interface. I wrote a couple of Basic language routines (surely nothing to brag about and added a power on light). I joined a Bally Newsletter, got one each month for several months (I think) and that's it. We had the Bally for a couple of years and bought all the cartridges that were released. I sold it to buy a PC but should have kept the Bally Computer. I'm not sure how many units they made before Bally sold the rights and the name was changed to 'Astrocade"? Well that's my experience with the Bally Astrocade. I saw a Bally on ebay a few days ago for sale. The asking price was $599. It looked new. I've seen a few others on ebay, most looked like junk.

I've always suggested removing the RF shielding from an Astrocade. What does your definition of "mostly working" mean?  Can you actually use the system to play a game? I think that Lance Squire mentioned that that great program is non y2K compliant!  What a shame!

 Here are some quick things you should check to see if they work properly:

1) Play included built-in programs.  Try running "Checkmate" with 0 players (the game will play itself).

2) Plug in a few carts.  Try them out.  Are you getting a good connection each time a cart is plugged in?  Unlike nearly all classic systems, the Astrocade does NOT need to be turned off when a cart is removed or inserted.  However, you will need to press "Reset" for a newly-inserted cart to work properly.  In fact, if you're new to the Astrocade, then you may be quite surprised to learn that some programs REQUIRE a cart to be removed while the program is running.  It's a neat trick and it allowed BASIC games to be put on carts.

3) Test all of the keypad keys (BASIC works well for this).

     I'm not sure if I ever posted here but as a newer member I thought I'd pass along my memories of the Bally Astrocade.

In 1977 I saw an ad in Popular Mechanics or some similar magazine. The ad was from JS&A, the original distributor of the Bally Home Library Computer. I ordered one but had to wait until 1978 to receive my first unit. The ad was very enticing.......remember this was 1977 before the PC. There were a couple of other game "consoles" but the Bally was neat. Try to erase anything about "computers" from your mind, then see an ad for the Bally "Computer".  Anyhow I received the "Bally Home Library Computer" opened the box and after an hour it started to fail. I sent it back to JS&A and got another unit. It began to fail in a couple of hours. I then got a 3rd unit. When the Bally was announced in 1977 there were delays one after another until they began to ship them in 1978. My recollection was the units did not meet FCC requirements until they installed a styrofoam shell covered with aluminum foil. Anyhow on the 3rd unit I threw the foil covers out and turned the Bally, waited a minute or so, touched each chip and found ( I think it was 3 chips running hot). I had some heat sinks ( I was a mainframe computer tech and had access to heat sinks) and glued them to the chips. No more heat problems. I added the Basic cartridge and the tape cassette interface. I wrote a couple of Basic language routines (surely nothing to brag about and added a power on light). I joined a Bally Newsletter, got one each month for several months (I think) and that's it. We had the Bally for a couple of years and bought all the cartridges that were released. I sold it to buy a PC but should have kept the Bally Computer. I'm not sure how many units they made before Bally sold the rights and the name was changed to 'Astrocade"? Well that's my experience with the Bally Astrocade. I saw a Bally on ebay a few days ago for sale. The asking price was $599. It looked new. I've seen a few others on ebay, most looked like junk.

What does your definition of "mostly working" mean?  Can you actually use the system to play a game?  How about the all-important function of computing your personal biorhythm using the must-own "Biorhythm" cart.  Oh, wait!  I think that Lance Squire mentioned that that great program is non y2K compliant!  What a shame!

 Here are some quick things you should check to see if they work properly:

1) Play included built-in programs.  Try running "Checkmate" with 0 players (the game will play itself).

2) Plug in a few carts.  Try them out.  Are you getting a good connection each time a cart is plugged in?  Unlike nearly all classic systems, the Astrocade does NOT need to be turned off when a cart is removed or inserted.  However, you will need to press "Reset" for a newly-inserted cart to work properly.  In fact, if you're new to the Astrocade, then you may be quite surprised to learn that some programs REQUIRE a cart to be removed while the program is running.  It's a neat trick and it allowed BASIC games to be put on carts.

3) Test all of the keypad keys (BASIC works well for this).

>>

>>

I presume that you mean the Atari 2600.  That's a great system.  If you can believe it, I never played "Yars' Revenge" until this week-- and now I've become semi-addicted to it under emulation.  I need to bring in my real system to play this great game.  One of my favorite games on the VCS (on any system, actually!) is Activision's "Beamrider."  Make sure to get your hands on that one!

If you're only now discovering classic systems, then maybe you haven't run into one of my other websites.  You will probably enjoy "Orphaned Computers and Game Systems"  too:

http://www.orphanedgames.com/

>>
how do you get those [BASIC games loaded] on the arcade?
>>

The BASIC games don't have to be moved to tape before they can be loaded on an Astrocade.  The programs on the original tapes have simply been saved as WAV files.  These AstroBASIC WAVs have usually been digitally archived and can be loaded straight into the AstroBASIC cartridge (with the built-in interface) from the PC.  However, there is a big gotcha here.  Make sure the output form the computer goes through speakers to give a boost to the audio, otherwise the sound will probably be too low for the Astrocade to "hear" it.

Here is an example of loading BASIC software.  First download a good game.  Here is a link to "The Pits," a great (but extremely simple looking game!) that has been previously archived.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_i-p/pits,_the_%5Brex_goulding%5D.zip

Take an audio cable from the output (usually the headphone jack) of the computer's speaker and insert the audio cable into the AstroBASIC cart.

On an Astrocade, insert the AstroBASIC cart and type:

:INPUT [Then press GO]

Then start playing the WAV file from the PC.  You should see the little LED on the BASIC cart light-up steadily.  If not, then adjust the volume controls until it does.  Sometimes it takes a little bit of trail and error, but once you get one program to load with the correct volume settings, then all programs will load with the same settings.

Adam

13850:
I added a "Code Translation Table" by Ed Horger to BallyAlley.com.

This is a code translation table for conversion between decimal, hex and binary. Ed created this so that he could program in machine language using the Bally BASIC cartridge.

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#CodeTranslationTableDoc

It's amazing how much work was involved to program in machine language via the Bally BASIC cartridge.  Anyone who programmed in ML and didn't own Blue Ram Utility was doing themselves a great disservice.  This typed document that Ed made looks like it was a lot of work to produce!  This kind of information is still useful, and you'll find this sort of information in the appendix of even some modern programming books

Adam
13851:
I added a previously unpublished article (from the Bob Fabris collection) called "Music Composer With Ears On And Edit (Compose by Ear)" by Larry Smith.

This program is designed to allow full usage of synthesizer functions at a relatively high speed (18 changes/sec) allowing up to 589 changes or entries, and also allowing the user to set up melody patterns first, and then "squeezing in" timings, or deleting mistakes, later. The notes being entered may be heard and compared against proceeding notes for correctness before being written. With all these functions, however, operations may be difficult at first, requiring a little practice.

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/basic.html#MusicComposerWithEarsOnAndEditDoc

People were always interested in trying to improve the sound that was available via BASIC on their Astrocade.  I'm not sure exactly when Larry Smith submitted this article to Bob Fabris (or if it was really even a proper submission for publication-- it could have just been written exclusively for Bob).  I bet that this article was written before George Moses and Brett Bilbrey began working together in earnest to try to get the best sound and music out of that little Arcade.

Adam
13852:
I added a previously unpublished article from the Bob Fabris Collection called "Machine Language Programming the Bally Arcade (Bare Bones-BASIC Only)" by Larry Smith.

The Z-80 operates on POKed in data, 16 bits at a time, two bytes in reverse order. For instance, if you had poked in the opcodes 0F D3, the processor reads it as D3 0F. Since Bally BASIC does not understand hex code, the opcodes must first be converted to decimal notation. Say you wanted to POKE in D5 00. First the bytes are swapped (00 D5), then the decimal value of the text digit is multiplied by its column position and the results added together.

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#MachineLanguageProgrammingtheBallyArcadeDoc

This article goes along with two programs that Larry also wrote: "Star Graphoids" and "Rainbow Display (Parts 1 and 2)"  These will be uploaded today.

Adam

13859:
The Arcadia 2001's hardware isn't nearly as flexible as the Bally Arcade-- but it's still a fun-- but, weird!-- system in its own way.  If you're into oddball consoles, then you can't go wrong with the Arcadia 2001: it's got some of the oddest history (what is known of it!) of all game consoles-- ever!  There is an Arcadia 2001 Yahoo group (although it's not really active much).

https://groups.yahoo.com/neo/groups/arcadia2001consoles/info

If you're not already familiar with the history of the Arcadia 2001, then Ward Shrake's Arcadia 2001 FAQ is an essential read:

http://www.digitpress.com/the_digs/arcadia/texts/2001-faq.htm

The FAQ hasn't been updated in well over a decade, but Ward was really the one who dived into the system and came up with the links to other compatible systems worldwide.  He made a multicart for the system which is indispensable to Arcadia 2001 owners (especially since most games were not released in a pin compatible format for the system).

The be-all-end-all site for Arcadia information is:

http://amigan.yatho.com/

This site reminds me of BallyAlley.com: it sure ain't pretty, but it's got the information that you're seeking.  It just takes some careful exploring to find it.

I suggest joining the Arcadia Yahoo group.  Quite a few members of this BallyAlley group are also members of that group (including myself).  If you're interested in talking about the Arcadia, then please join-up there and chat with other like-minded collectors.

I have a suggestion about system collecting that I learned the hard way over the years: find a system or two that you like best and concentrate on that/those system(s).  There are hundreds of computers and game systems that have been released over the years.  If you spread yourself thin, then you won't be able to enjoy what each system has to offer.  It's easy to buy dozens of systems-- but it's not easy to really learn much about all of those different systems.

I concentrate on two systems: the Atari 8-Bit computers (because of the hundreds of great games) and the Bally Arcade (because its rich history and early hacker-ethic/computer culture).  This has worked well for me.  Surely, I play around with other systems (classic and semi-modern) too, but I've decided that learning about and actually actively using a system brings the most enjoyment to me.

Adam

I added "Arcadian RDOS 1.0" by Stu Haigh to BallyAlley.com.  This DOS was written for the Bally Arcade in 1980.

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#ArcadianRDOSSourceCode

This is a CP/M compatible resident Disk Operating System. This code is designed to interface into the Cromemco software system and is provided with an autoload feature that will load track zero, sector zero of Drive A starting at RAM location 0080. Control will then be passed to the just loaded code at location 0080.

The code uses a 5501 as a COM. controller and a 1771 Flex Disk controller. It will support four 5 1/4", or two 5 1/4" and one 9", or two 9" disk drives.

The photocopied datasheets that were included with Stu's RDOS source code have been scanned and are also available:

1) TMS 5501 I/O Controller
2) Western Digital FD1771 A/B 01-02 Floppy Disk Formatter/Controller
3) Western Digital FD1771 Floppy Disk Formatter/Controller

This DOS is just another incredible example of what the Bally Arcade software/hardware hackers were able to make their little Bally systems do!

> as keyboards, cd or dvd disk drives, light pens?
>

You usually need a BASIC cart to use any of the tape interfaces. The later AstroBASIC came with the tape interface built in.(2000 baud)

The Earlier Bally BASIC had an external tape interface that plugged into the Light Pen and Controller 4 ports. it was only 300 baud.

Either can be connected to Cassette tape players, Media Players, CD or even Computer to transfer the data into or out of the unit.

The trick is finding the right volume level. Enough to light the LED, but not so much as to overpower it.

You can still find "Shoebox" tape recorders if you look. However, most people would prefer to hook it up to their computer and use the extensive list of programs already on BallyAlley.

the bids others have placed. The amount only goes as high as the next

as the current bid. It won't pass $50 until someone bids over $50.

Unfortunately, When someone else tried the same trick with $4000, or actually had serious money and really wanted it, the poor guy who tried to make the sure win found they couldn't cover the now winning bid.

Some other people try to 'Ninja' the system by putting in their higher bid seconds before it closes. Some use programs to do this. Hoping to find the wining number without revealing their top bid.

Of course, that's pointless when someone has already bid more than you are willing to pay.

So, my strategy is to simply bid what I'm willing to shell out for it.
If I'm out-bid, they had more $ and wanted it more.
If not, I'm happy as I got it as a price I thought it was worth.

However, I must admit I haven't played recently, as the starting prices on most things I'm interested in are way too high. Even if I did have that kind of money.

I added three extended BASIC programs:

Archiving notes by Paul Thacker: "Found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled: ' 300 BAUD COPY TEST RUN FROM UTIL (GOSUB 7000) 6000 BYTE IN 7040.' http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#CopyTestXB

2) "Cylon Raiders" (mod)

This game has been modified for use with Blue Ram BASIC.  The 300-baud Bally BASIC version of this game is on W&&W Software Sales' Tape 4.  The modified version is from Ken Lill's tape collection.  This game was among Cylon Raiders, Pack-Rat, and Artillery Duel all on one hand-labeled tape with a George Moses label.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#CylonRaidersXB

Originally by Dave Martin, this version has been modified by Dave Carson for Blue Ram BASIC.  The AstroBASIC game was released in ARCADIAN 3 no. 10 (August 12, 1981): 106,107.

I added "Rebound" (Mod) by Dave Martin (modified by Bruce Brigden).  This 2000 baud, Blue RAM BASIC program was modified in the 1980s.  The original AstroBASIC program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 12 (Oct. 05, 1981): 124. and was reprinted in ARCADIAN 6, no. 6 (Apr. 20, 1984): 54.

This Blue RAM BASIC version of "Rebound" was never published. The AstroBASIC version of "Rebound" was the $100 contest winner for October 1981. These are the game instructions from the October 1981 issue of the "Arcadian" newsletter:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#ReboundXB

Here are the instructions from "Arcadian" for the AstroBASIC version of the game:

"Rebound" is a game of skill for one player. Turn knob to select ball speed (0- fast 5-very slow) and pull trigger. You try to clear as many diamonds as possible off the board using a ball that may only be controlled as it bounces off the wall. Use joystick when ball approaches a wall to tell it to bounce (45 degrees) on the right, left, up, or down. You must hold joystick position until after ball has bounced off the wall.

If you clear the board, you are challenged to clear a second and third board. On the second board, one diamond is marked and will flash before you begin. If you do not erase this one last, the game is over. On the third board, one diamond will flash, but is not marked. You must remember this one to erase it last!

A couple more catches: points are deducted for crossing a path you have already traveled, and finally, you cannot bounce into a corner, or the game ends.


Have fun!

13916:
Today, I was sorting through Bally BASIC type-in programs that need to be added from my local drive to BallyAlley.com.  One of the type-in programs is a programming language by Bob Wiseman called "Bally Forth."  This program was never printed, and has yet to be archived.  "Bally Forth" was originally submitted (on the same tape) with "Tower of Hanoi."

I originally added "Tower of Hanoi" to BallyAlley.com on February 27, 2006.    As was my normal routine in the early-days of adding programs to the wbsite, in order to save time I didn't added any information about the game when it was uploaded to BallyAlley.com.

You can download the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#TowerofHanoiAB

"Tower of Hanoi"
By Bob Wiseman
ARCADIAN 3, no. 5 (Mar. 07, 1981): 53-54. (Bally BASIC version)
ARCADIAN 6, no. 10 (Aug. 24, 1984): 94. (Reprint, for AstroBASIC)

This game was submitted to the "Arcadian" on January 12, 1981. Instructions from the original printing of the game:


"Tower of Hanoi" is an old game, originally played with a set of rings to be placed on three pegs mounted on a board.  The number of moves required to shift the pile from one location to the final location is equal to 2 -1, where n is the number of blocks.  For a four-block pile then, the minimum number of moves is 15.  I dug into an old Johnson-Smith catalog to find the puzzle available there for 35 cents, but the catalog is 40 years old...

The object of this puzzle is to rebuild the Tower of Hanoi in a new location.  You will be asked how many blocks you wish, and these will be stacked in descending order on the left.  Now you must move them around to rebuild the tower in the center or on the right.  A larger block may not rest on a smaller block.

Moving a block is done in two stages.  First, you erase it, then you redraw it. Only the top block of a stack may be moved.  To indicate which stack you want, use the hand control.


Instructions from Bob Wiseman's original program submission letter to the "Arcadian:"


You will be asked how many boxes you want in the stack.  Please answer through the keyboard with a number from 2 to 7.  The object is to restack these boxes in the center or on the right.

The restacking is done by lifting a box and setting it down.

A larger box may not be placed on a smaller box.  To indicate which stack you want to lift from or place on use control number one. JX = -1 indicates the left stack, JY = +1 is for the center , and JX = +1 is for the right stack. You will be rated at the end, and you will be given one more box to play with.


I think that "Tower of Hanoi" is a good fit for Bally BASIC.  It doesn't require smooth animation or a fast programming language.  Games like this are the ones that BASIC, on any platform, is able to excel at creating.

13917:
I added a Bally BASIC type-in program, from 1981, called "Bally Forth" by Bob Wiseman.  This program has not yet been archived in downloadable format.  However, since "Tower of Hanoi" was submitted on the same tape, I presume that Paul can probably digitally archive this program from a tape he has already recorded.

Bob Wiseman notes, "This is a simple Forth-like language which is interpreted by Bally
BASIC. It is very different from BASIC and some mental reprogramming may
 be necessary."

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallyForthBASICType-In

This is an unpublished program submission to the "Arcadian."  However, Bob Fabris must have originally meant to print the program in the newsletter, because it was laid-out in his standard fashion-- as can be seen in the above scanned document.

Bob Wiseman made rather extensive documentation for "Bally Forth," some of which I've OCRed here.

I hope that I offend no one by calling this "Forth". The similarities are present but are limited. Please understand that this is an eensy-weensy version. Nonetheless, for those of you wishing a new challenge, a change of pace from the vulgarities of Tiny BASIC, here is a new language that you can fret over.

This language operates on a stack principle. You do not have any data names (like "a"), you have a stack of data, much like a stack of playing cards. First you enter your program and your program creates and manipulates this stack of numbers.

Each number in the stack must be a number that is valid in Bally BASIC. These are stored in the at-sign string, but more about this later. First, let us look at the operations that are available.


People who love the unusual qualities of the Bally Arcade-- the oddness about the system that separates it from other consoles of its generation-- will enjoy "Bally Forth."  Running a limited, slow Forth (written in Bally BASIC!) helps to illuminate to us modern users that Bally Arcade owners had many interests-- and, for early users at least, games may not have been the primary motivation for purchasing the Bally Arcade in the 1970s.

13918:
I added the original program submission letter to the "Arcadian" along with the commented hand-written BASIC listing for the game "Bagels" by Carl Morimoto.  This program was first published in ARCADIAN 2, no. 3 (Jan. 15, 1980): 25.  It was later republished in "Arcadian Sampler Programs."

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#BagelsAB

Today, I OCRed and proofread the instructions from the program's original publication in the "Arcadian" newsletter.

"Bagels" is a game in which a player, using logical deduction, predicts a given number.  In this version, the number is a random 3 digits with no duplicating digits, and after each guess the program displays one of the following responses:

BAGELS - No digit is correct

PICO - One correct digit is in the wrong place

PICO-PICO - Two or more correct digits are in the wrong places

FERMI - One correct digit is in the correct place

FERMI-PICO - One correct digit is in the correct place and one or more Correct digit is in the wrong place

FERMI-FERMI - Two or more correct digits are in the correct places

Since the correctness of only two out of three digits is disclosed, after the FERMI-FERMI response the program prompts for the confirmation of the last entry as the player's choice by printing GAME GUESS?

Press GO when the player believes that it is the true number. Press any other key to continue entering more guesses.

The program then displays whether the player's choice was right or wrong. When at least one game is won, game statistics will print after each game.

Press GO to start the next game.

A running average is computed as the total number of guesses divided by the number of games won.

Enter 000 to give up guessing the number and to proceed to the next game with a new number. The discontinued game is not considered as a lost game, but the number of guesses (not including the 000 entry) for the current game contributes to the game average.

Use the ERASE key for re-entering the first two digits. When the third digit is entered, the program immediately displays one of the responses.

Good luck and have fun with BAGELS.

Adam

Chuck Zellers wrote:

>>

I  just bought a new Bally Arcade

Congratulations!  How long has it been since you've owned a Bally Arcade system, Chuck?  35 years or so?

Here are some add-on suggestions for the Astrocade:


1) First, make sure that the Astrocade works correctly.  Check all four game ports.


2) Get a copy of the BASIC cartridge with the built-in 2000-baud tape interface.  Many Astrocades seem to come with this cart.  If you don't have one, then let me know.  I have some new-old stock AstroBASIC carts that I sell for a reasonable price.


3) If you don't have any carts, then get some that you used to play.  The cheapest carts for any classic game system, are generally, usually among the best games.  This makes sense because the fun games sold better than the lousy games, and thus they are more common.


4) Can't decide on a game?  Then give "Incredible Wizard" of "Galactic Invasion" a whirl.  You can't go wrong with either of those stand-by games.


5) Try loading (and saving?) some BASIC programs.


Before you try to get any additional Astrocade hardware, get reacquainted with the Bally Arcade system.  Investigate the fun of the console.  Let your needs dictate what software/hardware that you might want, rather than just getting hardware because someone recommends it.


Finally, now that you're waiting for your Astrocade to arrive in the mail, sit back and watch all of the Astrocade review videos made by Nice & Games:


https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=nice+and+games+astrocade


Good luck and... have fun!


Adam
